slides.title: In 1518, a city tried to cure a dancing plague with music.
It started with one woman
slides.body: In July 1518 a woman recorded as Frau Troffea began dancing in a Strasbourg street and kept going for days.

slides.title: Then the others joined
slides.body: Within weeks others had joined her. Chronicles put the number of dancers that summer anywhere from about 50 to 400.

slides.title: Doctor's orders: keep dancing
slides.body: Physicians blamed overheated blood, so the council opened guildhalls, hired musicians and paid strong men to hold the dancers up.

slides.title: Plan B: Saint Vitus
slides.body: As numbers grew, it banned public music and dancing and sent the dancers to a Saint Vitus shrine, where priests used crosses, holy water and red shoes.

slides.title: The death toll may be a myth
slides.body: Retellings claim 15 deaths a day. That's unproven: the 1518 records don't clearly mention any deaths. One historian reads it as mass psychogenic illness.

caption: The first cure was more dancing: hired musicians, open guildhalls and strong men to hold the dancers up. Numbers kept growing. What would you have tried?
